Galápagos is home to 28,583 residents living on only 3 percent of the land, while 97 percent is protected national park. To safeguard this fragile volcanic ecosystem and its finite resources—where most food arrives on cargo ships from Guayaquil and tap water is brackish—Ecuador enforces strict internal border controls. Mainland citizens may visit for only sixty days a year, and gaining permanent residency requires being born to a resident or undergoing a rigorous ten-year marriage verification. Supporters emphasize that without strict population limits, island infrastructure and unique wildlife cannot survive. On the other side, critics note that Ecuador's constitution guarantees freedom of movement, arguing that citizens from Quito or Guayaquil should have the right to live and work in any province of their own country. When protecting a world heritage ecosystem clashes with the constitutional freedom of movement, which principle should come first? Which side do you lean toward, and why? Tell us where you are watching from today. 👇
